claim: RNA-seq analysis of MDA-MB-231 cells showed 1151 genes were significantly upregulated and 310 genes were downregulated under hypoxic stress (adjusted p<0.05).
source: Differential expression analysis showed that 1151 genes were significantly upregulated and 310 genes were downregulated (adjusted p<0.05) under hypoxic stress (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Upregulated genes under hypoxic stress were related to pathways of cell proliferation and cancer.
source: Enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes by Metascape suggested that the upregulated genes were related to the pathways of cell proliferation and cancer; in contrast, the downregulated genes were implicated in the DNA damage repair, senescence, SIRT1, and p53 signaling pathways (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Metascape enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Downregulated genes under hypoxic stress were implicated in DNA damage repair, senescence, SIRT1, and p53 signaling pathways.
source: Enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes by Metascape suggested that the upregulated genes were related to the pathways of cell proliferation and cancer; in contrast, the downregulated genes were implicated in the DNA damage repair, senescence, SIRT1, and p53 signaling pathways (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Metascape enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The stabilities of SIRT1 and p53 protein were not changed under hypoxia.
source: To further investigate the mechanism by which hypoxia regulates the p53 signaling pathway, we examined p53 pathway activity by Western blotting and found that the stabilities of SIRT1 and p53 protein were not changed under hypoxia, but the acetylation of p53 was decreased (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The acetylation of p53 was decreased under hypoxia.
source: To further investigate the mechanism by which hypoxia regulates the p53 signaling pathway, we examined p53 pathway activity by Western blotting and found that the stabilities of SIRT1 and p53 protein were not changed under hypoxia, but the acetylation of p53 was decreased (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The protein level of DBC1 gradually decreased with the duration of hypoxia.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the protein level of DBC1 gradually decreased with the duration of hypoxia (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing time-dependent decrease in DBC1 protein levels under hypoxia in Figure 1D.

claim: Hypoxia-induced decrease in DBC1 protein level was not blocked by HIF1α inhibitor.
source: The results showed that hypoxia-induced decrease in DBC1 protein level and p53 signaling pathway activity was not blocked by HIF1α inhibitor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data with HIF1α inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HIF1α signaling pathway is not involved in hypoxia-induced decrease in DBC1.
source: These results prove that HIF1α signaling pathway is not involved in hypoxia-induced decrease in DBC1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing HIF1α inhibitor did not block DBC1 decrease.

claim: The decrease in DBC1 protein level under hypoxic conditions could be inhibited by the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, the decrease in DBC1 protein level could be inhibited by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 1E), but not the lysosomal inhibitor BA1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that hypoxia induced DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing MG132 treatment prevents DBC1 degradation under hypoxia in Figure 1E.

claim: The decrease in DBC1 protein level under hypoxic conditions was not inhibited by the lysosomal inhibitor BA1.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, the decrease in DBC1 protein level could be inhibited by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 1E), but not the lysosomal inhibitor BA1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that hypoxia induced DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing BA1 treatment does not prevent DBC1 degradation under hypoxia in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Hypoxia induced DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, the decrease in DBC1 protein level could be inhibited by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 1E), but not the lysosomal inhibitor BA1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that hypoxia induced DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing MG132 but not BA1 prevents DBC1 degradation under hypoxia.

claim: DBC1 protein was degraded under hypoxia in most cell lines derived from different subtypes of breast cancer or other cancers.
source: In most cell lines derived from different subtypes of breast cancer or other cancers, DBC1 protein was degraded under hypoxia, suggesting the reduced stability of DBC1 was a general rule in hypoxic conditions (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1), while the mRNA level of CCAR2 was not changed under hypoxia (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data from multiple cell lines shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The reduced stability of DBC1 was a general rule in hypoxic conditions.
source: In most cell lines derived from different subtypes of breast cancer or other cancers, DBC1 protein was degraded under hypoxia, suggesting the reduced stability of DBC1 was a general rule in hypoxic conditions (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1), while the mRNA level of CCAR2 was not changed under hypoxia (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing DBC1 degradation across multiple cell lines under hypoxia.

claim: The mRNA level of CCAR2 was not changed under hypoxia.
source: In most cell lines derived from different subtypes of breast cancer or other cancers, DBC1 protein was degraded under hypoxia, suggesting the reduced stability of DBC1 was a general rule in hypoxic conditions (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1), while the mRNA level of CCAR2 was not changed under hypoxia (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Genes related to cell proliferation and migration were upregulated in CCAR2 knockout MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Similarly, the RNA-seq datasets of CCAR2 knockout MDA-MB-231 cells showed that genes related to cell proliferation and migration were also upregulated, and genes associated with DNA repair and apoptosis were downregulated (Figure 1H and I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from CCAR2 knockout cells shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Genes associated with DNA repair and apoptosis were downregulated in CCAR2 knockout MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Similarly, the RNA-seq datasets of CCAR2 knockout MDA-MB-231 cells showed that genes related to cell proliferation and migration were also upregulated, and genes associated with DNA repair and apoptosis were downregulated (Figure 1H and I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from CCAR2 knockout cells shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Hypoxia and DBC1 degradation contribute to tumor progression.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that hypoxia and DBC1 degradation contribute to tumor progression, which suggests that hypoxia may regulate tumor progression by mediating DBC1 protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA-seq data showing similar pathway changes in hypoxia and DBC1 knockout conditions.

claim: Hypoxia may regulate tumor progression by mediating DBC1 protein degradation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that hypoxia and DBC1 degradation contribute to tumor progression, which suggests that hypoxia may regulate tumor progression by mediating DBC1 protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observed correlation between hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation and tumor-related pathway changes.

claim: SIAH2 was identified to be responsible for the stability of DBC1.
source: To identify the E3 ligases that potentially ubiquitinates DBC1 to contribute to its degradation, several ubiquitin E3 ligases previously reported to be involved in the hypoxia response were screened (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and SIAH2 was finally identified to be responsible for the stability of DBC1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by screening data shown in Figure 2A and 2B identifying SIAH2 as the E3 ligase affecting DBC1 stability.

claim: DBC1 was validated as one of the substrates of SIAH2 by LC-MS/MS analysis.
source: To confirm our hypothesis, LC-MS/MS analysis of proteins bound to SIAH2RM (an SIAH2 enzyme-inactive mutant) was performed. DBC1 was validated as one of the substrates of SIAH2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS proteomic analysis identifying DBC1 in SIAH2RM-bound proteins.

claim: Exogenously expressed Flag-SIAH2RM and Myc-DBC1 were reciprocally co-immunoprecipitated.
source: To further explore the relationship between SIAH2 and DBC1, we carried out a co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay and found that exogenously expressed Flag-SIAH2RM and Myc-DBC1 were reciprocally co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Endogenous SIAH2 and DBC1 interact.
source: Meanwhile, we validated the interaction between endogenous SIAH2 and DBC1 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), and purified glutathione S-transferase (GST) SIAH2 was able to pull down His-DBC1 in vitro (Figure 2E), suggesting that DBC1 could directly interact with SIAH2.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: DBC1 could directly interact with SIAH2.
source: Meanwhile, we validated the interaction between endogenous SIAH2 and DBC1 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), and purified glutathione S-transferase (GST) SIAH2 was able to pull down His-DBC1 in vitro (Figure 2E), suggesting that DBC1 could directly interact with SIAH2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vitro GST pull-down assay showing direct binding between purified SIAH2 and DBC1 proteins in Figure 2E.

claim: The 1–230 amino acids at the N-terminus of DBC1 were necessary for binding to SIAH2.
source: To identify the necessary domain of DBC1 responsible for interaction with SIAH2, we constructed several truncations of DBC1 and SIAH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), and the Co-IP assay showed that the 1–230 amino acids at the N-terminus of DBC1 were necessary for binding to SIAH2 (Figure 2F), and the full-length SIAH2 was required for their interaction (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with DBC1 truncation mutants shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The full-length SIAH2 was required for interaction with DBC1.
source: To identify the necessary domain of DBC1 responsible for interaction with SIAH2, we constructed several truncations of DBC1 and SIAH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), and the Co-IP assay showed that the 1–230 amino acids at the N-terminus of DBC1 were necessary for binding to SIAH2 (Figure 2F), and the full-length SIAH2 was required for their interaction (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with SIAH2 truncation mutants shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The N-terminus (1–461) of the DBC1 protein rather than the C-terminus (462–923) was pulled down by SIAH2 in vitro.
source: Importantly, the N-terminus (1–461) of the DBC1 protein rather than the C-terminus (462–923) was pulled down by SIAH2 in vitro (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: The N-terminus of DBC1 is crucial for its interaction with SIAH2.
source: These results suggest that the N-terminus of DBC1 is crucial for its interaction with SIAH2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing the N-terminal region of DBC1 is necessary and sufficient for SIAH2 binding.

claim: SIAH2, rather than SIAH2RM, reduced the protein level of endogenous DBC1 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In line with the fact that SIAH2 acts as an E3 ligase, mediating substrate degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, we found that SIAH2, rather than SIAH2RM, reduced the protein level of endogenous DBC1 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2J and M) and had no effect on the transcriptional level of DBC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing dose-dependent DBC1 reduction with SIAH2 but not SIAH2RM in Figure 2J and M.

claim: SIAH2 had no effect on the transcriptional level of DBC1.
source: In line with the fact that SIAH2 acts as an E3 ligase, mediating substrate degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, we found that SIAH2, rather than SIAH2RM, reduced the protein level of endogenous DBC1 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2J and M) and had no effect on the transcriptional level of DBC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Ectopic expression of wildtype SIAH2, but not SIAH2RM, promoted DBC1 degradation over time.
source: The CHX chase assay showed that ectopic expression of wildtype SIAH2, but not SIAH2RM, promoted DBC1 degradation over time (Figure 2K and L and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG132 completely reversed DBC1 destabilization.
source: Furthermore, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 completely reversed DBC1 destabilization (Figure 2N), whereas the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BA1) had no such function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that SIAH2 mediated DBC1 degradation through the proteasome pathway rather than lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing MG132 prevents SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation in Figure 2N.

claim: The lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BA1) did not reverse DBC1 destabilization.
source: Furthermore, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 completely reversed DBC1 destabilization (Figure 2N), whereas the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BA1) had no such function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that SIAH2 mediated DBC1 degradation through the proteasome pathway rather than lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing BA1 does not prevent SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: SIAH2 mediated DBC1 degradation through the proteasome pathway rather than lysosomes.
source: Furthermore, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 completely reversed DBC1 destabilization (Figure 2N), whereas the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BA1) had no such function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that SIAH2 mediated DBC1 degradation through the proteasome pathway rather than lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing MG132 but not BA1 prevents SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation.

claim: SIAH2 promotes DBC1 degradation by directly interacting with DBC1.
source: These results reveal that SIAH2 promotes DBC1 degradation by directly interacting with DBC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing SIAH2-DBC1 interaction and SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation.

claim: Ectopic expression of SIAH2, but not SIAH2RM, dramatically increased the ubiquitination level of DBC1.
source: Next, we checked whether SIAH2 ubiquitinated DBC1, and the results showed that ectopic expression of SIAH2, but not SIAH2RM, dramatically increased the ubiquitination level of DBC1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: SIAH2 induced the polyubiquitination of DBC1 in the form of K48 conjugation.
source: Additionally, immunoprecipitation analysis proved that SIAH2 induced the polyubiquitination of DBC1 in the form of K48 conjugation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay with K48-specific ubiquitin shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: DBC1 was directly ubiquitinated by SIAH2 rather than the E3 ligase-dead mutant SIAH2RM in vitro.
source: In vitro ubiquitination assay further revealed that DBC1 was directly ubiquitinated by SIAH2 rather than the E3 ligase-dead mutant SIAH2RM (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: K287 of DBC1 was the potential site ubiquitinated by SIAH2.
source: To identify the sites of DBC1 ubiquitinated by SIAH2, we performed MS analysis, and the results showed that K287 of DBC1 was the potential site ubiquitinated by SIAH2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis identifying ubiquitinated K287 shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ectopic expression of SIAH2 did not increase the ubiquitination level of the K287R mutant of DBC1.
source: Next, we found that ectopic expression of SIAH2 did not increase the ubiquitination level of the K287R mutant of DBC1, and the mutant did not degrade (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data with DBC1 K287R mutant shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: The K287R mutant of DBC1 did not degrade.
source: Next, we found that ectopic expression of SIAH2 did not increase the ubiquitination level of the K287R mutant of DBC1, and the mutant did not degrade (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing K287R mutant is resistant to SIAH2-mediated degradation in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: SIAH2 ubiquitinates DBC1 to mediate its degradation.
source: In conclusion, these results demonstrate that SIAH2 ubiquitinates DBC1 to mediate its degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation.

claim: Under hypoxic stress both SIAH2 deletion and K287R mutation of DBC1 failed to increase DBC1 ubiquitination.
source: To further understand the mechanism underlying hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation, we examined whether SIAH2 was responsible for DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation in response to hypoxia. Our results showed that under hypoxic stress both SIAH2 deletion and K287R mutation of DBC1 failed to increase DBC1 ubiquitination (Figure 3F and G), and DBC1 degradation was also inhibited (Figure 3H–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data under hypoxia with SIAH2 knockout or DBC1 K287R mutant shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Under hypoxic stress, DBC1 degradation was inhibited by SIAH2 deletion and K287R mutation of DBC1.
source: To further understand the mechanism underlying hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation, we examined whether SIAH2 was responsible for DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation in response to hypoxia. Our results showed that under hypoxic stress both SIAH2 deletion and K287R mutation of DBC1 failed to increase DBC1 ubiquitination (Figure 3F and G), and DBC1 degradation was also inhibited (Figure 3H–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing DBC1 protein levels are maintained under hypoxia in SIAH2 knockout or with K287R mutant in Figure 3H-J and supplementary figures.

claim: Knockout of SIAH2 prolonged the half-life of DBC1 under hypoxia.
source: Consistently, knockout of SIAH2 prolonged the half-life of DBC1 under hypoxia (Figure 3K and L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data in SIAH2 knockout cells under hypoxia shown in Figure 3K and L and supplementary figures.

claim: SIAH2 could be phosphorylated by kinases such as p38 and Src under hypoxic conditions, increasing its ubiquitin ligase activity and protein stability.
source: It has been reported that under hypoxic conditions the regulation of SIAH2 was regulated by several mechanisms including induction of gene expression, interference translation, and formation of dimeric complexes. SIAH2 could be phosphorylated by kinases such as p38 and Src under hypoxic conditions, increasing its ubiquitin ligase activity and protein stability (Khurana et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Khurana et al., 2006).

claim: Inhibition of p38 partially decreased SIAH2 protein level under hypoxia.
source: Moreover, we found that inhibition of p38 partially decreased SIAH2 protein level and inhibited the interaction between SIAH2 and DBC1 under hypoxia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data with p38 inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Inhibition of p38 inhibited the interaction between SIAH2 and DBC1 under hypoxia.
source: Moreover, we found that inhibition of p38 partially decreased SIAH2 protein level and inhibited the interaction between SIAH2 and DBC1 under hypoxia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with p38 inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Hypoxia activates SIAH2 to interact with DBC1, which induces DBC1 degradation by ubiquitin–proteasome system to regulate DBC1 stability.
source: Therefore, hypoxia activates SIAH2 to interact with DBC1, which induces DBC1 degradation by ubiquitin–proteasome system to regulate DBC1 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing hypoxia-induced SIAH2-DBC1 interaction and DBC1 degradation.

claim: Hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation is dependent on SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation is dependent on SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing SIAH2 is required for hypoxia-induced DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation.

claim: The ubiquitination level of DBC1 was sharply decreased when returned to normal conditions after hypoxic stress.
source: Strikingly, we also observed that the ubiquitination level of DBC1 was sharply decreased when returned to normal conditions after hypoxic stress (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data showing reduced DBC1 ubiquitination after reoxygenation in Figure 4A.

claim: OTUD5 might interact with DBC1.
source: Therefore, we screened the deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) plasmids library to identify the candidate responsible for deubiquitination of DBC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Lots of interaction assays suggested that the potential DUB OTUD5 might interact with DBC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and regulate its ubiquitination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by screening and interaction assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: OTUD5 might regulate DBC1 ubiquitination.
source: Therefore, we screened the deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) plasmids library to identify the candidate responsible for deubiquitination of DBC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Lots of interaction assays suggested that the potential DUB OTUD5 might interact with DBC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and regulate its ubiquitination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data with OTUD5 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Endogenous DBC1 could directly interact with OTUD5.
source: Co-IP analysis demonstrated the exogenous interaction between OTUD5 and DBC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E). Furthermore, we confirmed that endogenous DBC1 could directly interact with OTUD5 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), which was further verified by an in vitro pull-down assay using purified His-tagged DBC1 to pull down OTUD5 from cell lysates (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data of endogenous proteins shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: Only ectopic expression of wildtype OTUD5 but not inactive mutant C224S led to DBC1 ubiquitination level decrease under hypoxia.
source: We next tested whether DBC1 deubiquitination was dependent on OTUD5 enzyme activity. The ubiquitination assay showed that only ectopic expression of wildtype OTUD5 but not inactive mutant C224S led to DBC1 ubiquitination level decrease under hypoxia (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data comparing wildtype and catalytically inactive OTUD5 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hypoxia-induced endogenous DBC1 degradation was specifically inhibited by expression of wildtype OTUD5 rather than the inactive mutant.
source: Consistently, hypoxia-induced endogenous DBC1 degradation was specifically inhibited by expression of wildtype OTUD5 rather than the inactive mutant (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing wildtype but not inactive OTUD5 prevents DBC1 degradation under hypoxia in Figure 4E.

claim: Ectopic expression of wildtype OTUD5 obviously prolonged the half-life of DBC1.
source: Moreover, the CHX assay also confirmed that ectopic expression of wildtype OTUD5 obviously prolonged the half-life of DBC1 (Figure 4F and G and Supplementary file 1), indicating that deubiquitination of DBC1 was beneficial for its stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data with OTUD5 overexpression shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Deubiquitination of DBC1 was beneficial for its stability.
source: Moreover, the CHX assay also confirmed that ectopic expression of wildtype OTUD5 obviously prolonged the half-life of DBC1 (Figure 4F and G and Supplementary file 1), indicating that deubiquitination of DBC1 was beneficial for its stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing OTUD5-mediated deubiquitination increases DBC1 half-life.

claim: The N-terminal region (amino acid residues 1–230) of DBC1 was necessary for its interaction with OTUD5.
source: Domain mapping analysis further revealed that the N-terminal region (amino acid residues 1–230) of DBC1, which binds with SIAH2, was also necessary for its interaction with OTUD5 (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with DBC1 truncation mutants shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Either hypoxia treatment or overexpression of SIAH2 promoted the interaction between DBC1 and SIAH2.
source: Interestingly, we found that either hypoxia treatment or overexpression of SIAH2 promoted the interaction between DBC1 and SIAH2, but inhibited the interaction of DBC1 with OTUD5 (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing increased DBC1-SIAH2 interaction under hypoxia or with SIAH2 overexpression in Figure 4I and supplementary figures.

claim: Either hypoxia treatment or overexpression of SIAH2 inhibited the interaction of DBC1 with OTUD5.
source: Interestingly, we found that either hypoxia treatment or overexpression of SIAH2 promoted the interaction between DBC1 and SIAH2, but inhibited the interaction of DBC1 with OTUD5 (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing decreased DBC1-OTUD5 interaction under hypoxia or with SIAH2 overexpression in Figure 4I and supplementary figures.

claim: SIAH2 and OTUD5 substitutionally interact with DBC1 in response to changes in oxygen concentration.
source: Overall, our results suggest that SIAH2 and OTUD5 substitutionally interact with DBC1 in response to changes in oxygen concentration (Figure 4J), cooperatively regulating reversible DBC1 ubiquitination and stability to orchestrate DBC1 function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing competitive binding of SIAH2 and OTUD5 to DBC1 under different oxygen conditions.

claim: SIAH2 and OTUD5 cooperatively regulate reversible DBC1 ubiquitination and stability to orchestrate DBC1 function.
source: Overall, our results suggest that SIAH2 and OTUD5 substitutionally interact with DBC1 in response to changes in oxygen concentration (Figure 4J), cooperatively regulating reversible DBC1 ubiquitination and stability to orchestrate DBC1 function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing SIAH2 ubiquitinates and OTUD5 deubiquitinates DBC1 in response to oxygen levels.

claim: Knockdown of SIAH2 attenuated the reduction of p53 pathway activity under hypoxia.
source: As suggested in Figure 1, hypoxia-induced DBC1 degradation might regulate pathways associated with tumor cell growth, such as SIRT1 and p53 signaling pathways. Therefore, we examined whether SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination was responsible for tumor progression. Our results showed that knockdown of SIAH2, in different breast cancer cell lines, attenuated the reduction of p53 pathway activity under hypoxia (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data showing p53 acetylation is maintained with SIAH2 knockdown under hypoxia in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of SIAH2 promoted etoposide triggering cell apoptosis under hypoxia.
source: In addition, deletion of SIAH2 promoted etoposide triggering cell apoptosis under hypoxia, which could be rescued by simultaneous knockout of CCAR2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figures.

claim: Simultaneous knockout of CCAR2 rescued the increased apoptosis caused by SIAH2 deletion under hypoxia.
source: In addition, deletion of SIAH2 promoted etoposide triggering cell apoptosis under hypoxia, which could be rescued by simultaneous knockout of CCAR2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry apoptosis assay data showing double knockout rescues apoptosis phenotype in Figure 5B and supplementary figures.

claim: Cell growth was suppressed when SIAH2 was deleted under hypoxia.
source: The clone formation assay further revealed that cell growth was suppressed when SIAH2 was deleted under hypoxia, whereas double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 almost did not inhibit cell growth (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 almost did not inhibit cell growth under hypoxia.
source: The clone formation assay further revealed that cell growth was suppressed when SIAH2 was deleted under hypoxia, whereas double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 almost did not inhibit cell growth (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data showing double knockout rescues growth phenotype in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Knockout of SIAH2 inhibited cell migration under hypoxia.
source: Transwell and scratch assays also revealed that knockout of SIAH2 inhibited cell migration under hypoxia rather than double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell and scratch assay data shown in Figure 5D and E and supplementary figures.

claim: Double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 did not inhibit cell migration under hypoxia.
source: Transwell and scratch assays also revealed that knockout of SIAH2 inhibited cell migration under hypoxia rather than double knockout of SIAH2 and CCAR2 (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell and scratch assay data showing double knockout rescues migration phenotype in Figure 5D and E and supplementary figures.

claim: SIAH2 promotes cell growth, proliferation, and migration in response to hypoxia by ubiquitinating DBC1 to induce DBC1 degradation.
source: These results suggest that SIAH2 promotes cell growth, proliferation, and migration in response to hypoxia by ubiquitinating DBC1 to induce DBC1 degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing SIAH2 knockout inhibits these processes and double knockout with DBC1 rescues them.

claim: Both tumor volume and tumor weight in nude mice transplanted with SIAH2 knockout cells were decreased.
source: To validate the effects of SIAH2-mediated DBC1 stability on tumorigenesis and tumor progression in vivo, we implanted SIAH2 knockout and SIAH2/CCAR2 double-knockout MDA-MB-231 cells into the mammary fat pads of BALB/c nude mice and then monitored tumor growth. The results showed that both tumor volume and tumor weight in the nude mice transplanted with SIAH2 knockout cells were decreased, whereas concurrent deficiency of SIAH2 and DBC1 restored tumor growth to a certain extent (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor measurements shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Concurrent deficiency of SIAH2 and DBC1 restored tumor growth to a certain extent.
source: To validate the effects of SIAH2-mediated DBC1 stability on tumorigenesis and tumor progression in vivo, we implanted SIAH2 knockout and SIAH2/CCAR2 double-knockout MDA-MB-231 cells into the mammary fat pads of BALB/c nude mice and then monitored tumor growth. The results showed that both tumor volume and tumor weight in the nude mice transplanted with SIAH2 knockout cells were decreased, whereas concurrent deficiency of SIAH2 and DBC1 restored tumor growth to a certain extent (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor measurements showing double knockout partially rescues tumor growth in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The number of Ki67-positive proliferative cells in SIAH2 knockout-implanted tumors was decreased compared with that in both wildtype and SIAH2/CCAR2 double-knockout xenografts.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the number of Ki67-positive proliferative cells in SIAH2 knockout-implanted tumors was decreased compared with that in both wildtype and SIAH2/CCAR2 double-knockout xenografts (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The results of EdU assay to detect the proliferation rate of tumor cells of different genotypes were consistent with immunohistochemical analysis.
source: Furthermore, the results of EdU assay to detect the proliferation rate of tumor cells of different genotypes were consistent with immunohistochemical analysis. (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5J and K.

claim: The SIAH2-DBC1 axis plays a critical role in promoting tumor progression.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate the critical role of the SIAH2-DBC1 axis in promoting tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vitro and in vivo data showing SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation promotes tumor cell growth and migration.

claim: The expression level of SIAH2 was significantly higher in most tumors than in adjacent normal tissues.
source: To evaluate whether the mechanism by which the SIAH2-DBC1 axis regulates tumor progression is relevant to human tumorigenesis and tumor progression. We analyzed RNA-sequencing data in TCGA (Cancer Genome Atlas) using TIMER, and the results demonstrated that the expression level of SIAH2 was significantly higher in most tumors than in adjacent normal tissues (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The expression of SIAH2 in breast cancers was higher than that in normal samples.
source: In particular, the expression of SIAH2 in breast cancers was higher than that in normal samples (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SIAH2 was positively correlated with tumor stage.
source: Analyzing the data from TCGA, we found that SIAH2 was positively correlated with tumor stage and number of lymph nodes, indicative of tumor malignancy (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis showing correlation with tumor stage in Figure 6C.

claim: SIAH2 was positively correlated with number of lymph nodes.
source: Analyzing the data from TCGA, we found that SIAH2 was positively correlated with tumor stage and number of lymph nodes, indicative of tumor malignancy (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA data analysis showing correlation with lymph node metastasis in Figure 6D.

claim: DBC1 and SIAH2 were negatively correlated in breast cancer tissue microarrays.
source: To further explore the clinical relevance of SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation, we analyzed the expression of SIAH2 and DBC1 in breast cancer tissue microarrays of patients. The immunohistochemistry results showed that DBC1 and SIAH2 were negatively correlated in this cohort (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), coincident with our finding that DBC1 was the substrate of SIAH2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry analysis of patient tissue microarrays shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: In human breast cancer tissue DBC1 expression was reduced in hypoxic regions.
source: We also found that in human breast cancer tissue DBC1 expression was reduced in hypoxic regions (Figure 6G), and the downregulation of DBC1 was found to be negatively correlated with clinical stage and the percentage of the Ki67-positive cell population (Figure 6H and I and Supplementary file 2), further indicating that under pathological conditions SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation are beneficial for tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced DBC1 in CAIX-positive hypoxic regions in Figure 6G.

claim: The downregulation of DBC1 was negatively correlated with clinical stage.
source: We also found that in human breast cancer tissue DBC1 expression was reduced in hypoxic regions (Figure 6G), and the downregulation of DBC1 was found to be negatively correlated with clinical stage and the percentage of the Ki67-positive cell population (Figure 6H and I and Supplementary file 2), further indicating that under pathological conditions SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation are beneficial for tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of patient tissue microarray data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The downregulation of DBC1 was negatively correlated with the percentage of the Ki67-positive cell population.
source: We also found that in human breast cancer tissue DBC1 expression was reduced in hypoxic regions (Figure 6G), and the downregulation of DBC1 was found to be negatively correlated with clinical stage and the percentage of the Ki67-positive cell population (Figure 6H and I and Supplementary file 2), further indicating that under pathological conditions SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation are beneficial for tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of patient tissue microarray data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Under pathological conditions SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation are beneficial for tumor progression.
source: We also found that in human breast cancer tissue DBC1 expression was reduced in hypoxic regions (Figure 6G), and the downregulation of DBC1 was found to be negatively correlated with clinical stage and the percentage of the Ki67-positive cell population (Figure 6H and I and Supplementary file 2), further indicating that under pathological conditions SIAH2-mediated DBC1 ubiquitination and degradation are beneficial for tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from clinical data showing DBC1 downregulation correlates with tumor progression markers.

claim: DBC1 has been characterized as a key regulator of physiological and pathophysiological activities, such as DNA damage, senescence, and tumorigenesis.
source: DBC1 has been characterized as a key regulator of physiological and pathophysiological activities, such as DNA damage, senescence, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about DBC1 function.

claim: Hypoxia promoted DBC1 to interact with SIAH2 but not OTUD5.
source: Mechanistically, hypoxia promoted DBC1 to interact with SIAH2 but not OTUD5, resulting in the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of DBC1 through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing differential binding under hypoxia.

claim: Hypoxia resulted in the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of DBC1 through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.
source: Mechanistically, hypoxia promoted DBC1 to interact with SIAH2 but not OTUD5, resulting in the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of DBC1 through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assays and proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: SIAH2 knockout inhibited tumor cell proliferation and migration.
source: SIAH2 knockout inhibited tumor cell proliferation and migration, which could be rescued by double knockout of SIAH2/CCAR2.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation, transwell, and xenograft data.

claim: Double knockout of SIAH2/CCAR2 rescued the inhibition of tumor cell proliferation and migration caused by SIAH2 knockout.
source: SIAH2 knockout inhibited tumor cell proliferation and migration, which could be rescued by double knockout of SIAH2/CCAR2.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation, transwell, and xenograft data showing rescue phenotype.

claim: The SIAH2/DBC1 axis was responsible for tumor progression under hypoxic stress.
source: Human tissue microarray analysis further revealed that the SIAH2/DBC1 axis was responsible for tumor progression under hypoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue microarray analysis showing correlation between SIAH2/DBC1 expression and tumor progression markers.

claim: Hypoxic stress plays an essential role in the progression and metastasis of many solid tumors.
source: Hypoxic stress or low oxygen tension, a major hallmark of the tumor microenvironment, plays an essential role in the progression and metastasis of many solid tumors (Cheng et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cheng et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019).

claim: Hypoxic stress attenuates tumorigenesis and progression by modulating the Hippo signaling pathway and mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Moreover, our previous studies have documented that hypoxic stress attenuates tumorigenesis and progression by modulating the Hippo signaling pathway and mitochondrial biogenesis (Ma et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Ma et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2019).

claim: DBC1 mediates p53 function by inhibiting the deacetylase activity of SIRT1.
source: DBC1 mediates p53 function not only by inhibiting the deacetylase activity of SIRT1, but also by inhibition of p53 ubiquitination and degradation (Qin et al., 2015; Akande et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Qin et al., 2015; Akande et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).

claim: DBC1 mediates p53 function by inhibition of p53 ubiquitination and degradation.
source: DBC1 mediates p53 function not only by inhibiting the deacetylase activity of SIRT1, but also by inhibition of p53 ubiquitination and degradation (Qin et al., 2015; Akande et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Qin et al., 2015; Akande et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).

claim: DBC1 can specifically inhibit deacetylase HDAC3 activity and alter its subcellular distribution, resulting in cell senescence.
source: In addition, DBC1 can specifically inhibit deacetylase HDAC3 activity and alter its subcellular distribution, resulting in cell senescence (Chini et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chini et al., 2010).

claim: Mice with a genetic deletion of CCAR2 exhibited more likely to spontaneously develop lung tumors, liver tumors, lymphomas, and teratomas and showed poor overall survival.
source: Most importantly, mice with a genetic deletion of CCAR2 exhibited more likely to spontaneously develop lung tumors, liver tumors, lymphomas, and teratomas and showed poor overall survival (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Qin et al., 2015).

claim: The downregulation of DBC1 highly correlates with poor prognosis and distant metastatic relapse in breast, colon, and prostate cancer patients.
source: Recently, the downregulation of DBC1 highly correlates with poor prognosis and distant metastatic relapse in breast, colon, and prostate cancer patients, and low levels of DBC1 determine tumor grade and metastasis (Won et al., 2015; Noguchi et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Won et al., 2015; Noguchi et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2013).

claim: Low levels of DBC1 determine tumor grade and metastasis.
source: Recently, the downregulation of DBC1 highly correlates with poor prognosis and distant metastatic relapse in breast, colon, and prostate cancer patients, and low levels of DBC1 determine tumor grade and metastasis (Won et al., 2015; Noguchi et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Won et al., 2015; Noguchi et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2013).

claim: SIAH2 mediates the ubiquitination and degradation of substrates, including PI3K, LATS2, Spry2, ACK1, and TYK2.
source: An abundance of evidence has shown that SIAH2 mediates the ubiquitination and degradation of substrates, including PI3K, LATS2, Spry2, ACK1, and TYK2 (Chan et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2016; Buchwald et al., 2013; Nadeau et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2014), in response to hypoxic stress to modulate multiple signaling pathways, such as the Hippo pathway, Ras signaling pathway, and STAT3 pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chan et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2016; Buchwald et al., 2013; Nadeau et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2014).

claim: DBC1 activity is regulated by multiple post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation, acetylation and sumoylation.
source: In general, DBC1 activity is regulated by multiple post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation (Magni et al., 2015; Zannini et al., 2012), acetylation (Zheng et al., 2013; Rajendran et al., 2019) and sumoylation (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Magni et al., 2015; Zannini et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2013; Rajendran et al., 2019; Park et al., 2014).

claim: SIAH2 can ubiquitinate DBC1 at Lys287 by binding to the N-terminus of DBC1.
source: Our group demonstrated for the first time that SIAH2 can also ubiquitinate DBC1 at Lys287 by binding to the N-terminus of DBC1, resulting in DBC1 degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, and that deletion of SIAH2 will block DBC1 degradation in response to hypoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry and mutagenesis data.

claim: Deletion of SIAH2 will block DBC1 degradation in response to hypoxic stress.
source: Our group demonstrated for the first time that SIAH2 can also ubiquitinate DBC1 at Lys287 by binding to the N-terminus of DBC1, resulting in DBC1 degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, and that deletion of SIAH2 will block DBC1 degradation in response to hypoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data in SIAH2 knockout cells under hypoxia.

claim: Stimulation of DBC1 transcription inhibits SIRT1 activity, contributing to TGF-β-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
source: It has been reported that DBC1 cooperates with SIRT1 to mediate different physiological functions within mammalian cells. For example, stimulation of DBC1 transcription inhibits SIRT1 activity, contributing to TGF-β-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chen et al., 2021).

claim: SIRT7 represses DBC1 transcription to promote thyroid tumorigenesis by binding to the promoter of DBC1.
source: Additionally, SIRT7 represses DBC1 transcription to promote thyroid tumorigenesis by binding to the promoter of DBC1 (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Li et al., 2019).

claim: DBC1 was found to play a role in upregulating glucose homeostasis-related genes, which are implicated in type 2 diabetes pathogenesis.
source: Recently, DBC1 was found to play a role in upregulating glucose homeostasis-related genes, which are implicated in type 2 diabetes pathogenesis (Basu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Basu et al., 2020).

claim: The decrease in p53 acetylation was accompanied by DBC1 degradation in hypoxia zone of breast tumor.
source: We also found that the decrease in p53 acetylation was accompanied by DBC1 degradation in hypoxia zone of breast tumor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunofluorescence data showing reduced DBC1 in hypoxic regions and Western blotting showing reduced p53 acetylation under hypoxia.

claim: Ubiquitination is a dynamic and reversible process cooperatively regulated by E3 ligases and DUBs.
source: In general, ubiquitination is a dynamic and reversible process cooperatively regulated by E3 ligases and DUBs (Li and Reverter, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Li and Reverter, 2021).

claim: The deubiquitinase OTUD5 could specifically cleave the polyubiquitin chains of DBC1 once hypoxic stress was removed.
source: In this study, we identified that the deubiquitinase OTUD5 could specifically cleave the polyubiquitin chains of DBC1 once hypoxic stress was removed.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data showing reduced DBC1 ubiquitination after reoxygenation and with OTUD5 expression.

claim: If OTUD5 was overexpressed under hypoxia, the ubiquitination and degradation of DBC1 would be inhibited.
source: If OTUD5 was overexpressed under hypoxia, the ubiquitination and degradation of DBC1 would be inhibited.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay and Western blotting data with OTUD5 overexpression under hypoxia.

claim: SIAH2 and OTUD5 competitively bind to DBC1 at the same N-terminal region.
source: Interestingly, we further confirmed that SIAH2 and OTUD5 competitively bind to DBC1 at the same N-terminal region, and hypoxia promotes the interaction of DBC1 with SIAH2 rather than OTUD5, resulting in ubiquitination and degradation of DBC1 to promote tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by domain mapping data showing both bind the N-terminus and co-IP data showing competitive binding.

claim: Hypoxia promotes the interaction of DBC1 with SIAH2 rather than OTUD5, resulting in ubiquitination and degradation of DBC1 to promote tumor progression.
source: Interestingly, we further confirmed that SIAH2 and OTUD5 competitively bind to DBC1 at the same N-terminal region, and hypoxia promotes the interaction of DBC1 with SIAH2 rather than OTUD5, resulting in ubiquitination and degradation of DBC1 to promote tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data showing differential binding under hypoxia and functional assays showing tumor promotion.

claim: OTUD5 controls cell survival and cell proliferation by deubiquitinating substrates.
source: It is well known that OTUD5 controls cell survival and cell proliferation by deubiquitinating substrates (Zhang et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021; Cho et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; de Vivo et al., 2019; Park et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021; Cho et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; de Vivo et al., 2019; Park et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2007).

claim: The activation of OTUD5-mediated DBC1 deubiquitination may suppress tumor growth.
source: Based on our findings and others', we speculate that the activation of OTUD5-mediated DBC1 deubiquitination may suppress tumor growth, which may provide a novel target for clinical tumor therapy.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observed effects of OTUD5 on DBC1 stability and tumor cell behavior.

claim: Hypoxia stimulates SIAH2 to ubiquitinate DBC1 and inhibit OTUD5-mediated DBC1 deubiquitination, resulting in DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.
source: Taken together, our study revealed that hypoxia stimulates SIAH2 to ubiquitinate DBC1 and inhibit OTUD5-mediated DBC1 deubiquitination, resulting in DBC1 degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The SIAH2-DBC1 axis is important in promoting tumor cell survival and migration.
source: Our results further address the importance of the SIAH2-DBC1 axis in promoting tumor cell survival and migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assays showing SIAH2-mediated DBC1 degradation promotes these processes.
